claim: Ants are one of the most ecologically successful groups in nature, being widespread and abundant in almost every terrestrial ecosystem.
source: Ants are one of the most ecologically successful groups in nature: they are widespread and abundant in almost every terrestrial ecosystem, and have been around for >140 million years (Moreau and Bell, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moreau and Bell, 2013

claim: Ants have been around for more than 140 million years.

claim: The ecological success of ants has been attributed to their social organization, particularly their division of labor.
source: This success has been attributed to their social organization, particularly their division of labor (Wilson, 1971).

claim: Ants have complex architecture.
source: The ants' high degree of social organization has allowed them to develop collective behaviors that have many similarities to human societies: ants have complex architecture, have true agriculture cultivating fungi for food and herding aphids, use antibiotics and wage war with each other (Hölldobler and Wilson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hölldobler and Wilson, 2009

claim: Ants have true agriculture, cultivating fungi for food and herding aphids.

evidence: Supported by citation to Hölldobler and Wilson, 2009

claim: Ants use antibiotics.

claim: Many collective behaviors in ant colonies are presumed to be the result of self-organization, in which complex colony-level patterns emerge from local interactions among workers following simple rules.
source: Many collective behaviors in ant colonies are presumed to be the result of self-organization, in which complex colony-level patterns emerge from local interactions among workers following simple rules (Beshers and Fewell, 2001; Bonabeau et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beshers and Fewell, 2001 and Bonabeau et al., 1997

claim: Interaction rates have been shown to influence decision making, task allocation and task intensity in ants and other social insects.
source: The rates of these interactions are particularly important, as they have been shown to influence decision making, task allocation and task intensity in ants and other social insects (Gordon and Mehdiabadi, 1999; Greene and Gordon, 2007; O'Donnell and Bulova, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon and Mehdiabadi, 1999; Greene and Gordon, 2007; O'Donnell and Bulova, 2007

claim: Interaction rates are typically thought to be density-dependent.
source: Interaction rates are typically thought to be density-dependent, implying that changes in colony size and density could significantly alter group dynamics (Pacala et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pacala et al., 1996

claim: Changes in colony size and density are a naturally occurring phenomenon that are part of the life cycle of wood dwelling social insects such as carpenter ants.
source: Changes in colony size and density are a naturally occurring phenomenon that are part of the life cycle of wood dwelling social insects such as carpenter ants.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about carpenter ant life cycles

claim: Carpenter ant colonies start with a single queen that moves into a small wooden cavity and lays eggs.
source: Colonies start with a single queen that moves into a small wooden cavity and lays eggs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about carpenter ant colony founding

claim: Once carpenter ant workers hatch, they have to excavate wood to enlarge the nest and allow for colony growth.
source: Once the workers hatch, they have to excavate wood to enlarge the nest and allow for colony growth.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about carpenter ant nest expansion

claim: Each subsequent brood cycle in carpenter ant colonies will lead to fluctuations in colony size and density.
source: Accordingly, each subsequent brood cycle will lead to fluctuations in colony size and density.
evidence: Logical inference from nest excavation and colony growth patterns

claim: Density changes can occur when workers discover an attractive nesting location and the colony decides to split into multiple nest sites and thus becomes polydomous.
source: Density changes can also occur when workers discover an attractive nesting location and the colony decides to split into multiple nest sites and thus becomes polydomous (Buczkowski, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buczkowski, 2011

claim: Ants may be able to regulate their interaction rates by forming clusters when density is low or by avoiding contact with nearby neighbors if density is high.
source: Indeed, a study that manipulated colony size and density by putting workers in various arena sizes found that ants may be able to regulate their interaction rates (as measured by counting contacts via antennae) by forming clusters when density is low or by avoiding contact with nearby neighbors if density is high (Gordon et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon et al., 1993

claim: Workers exhibit distinct movement zones, that is 'spatial fidelity zones'.
source: Workers are known to exhibit distinct movement zones, that is 'spatial fidelity zones' (Sendova-Franks and Franks, 1995), which have been linked to an individual's behavioral repertoire in a variety of social insects (Baracchi and Cini, 2014; Heyman et al., 2017; Jandt and Dornhaus, 2009; Mersch et al., 2013; Powell and Tschinkel, 1999; Robson et al., 2000; Seeley, 1982).

evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Spatial fidelity zones are thought to play a key role in the development of the division of labor by promoting task specialization and reducing task switching costs.

source: Its primary function, the fast and efficient transfer of liquid food via regurgitation among colony members, is crucial because only a few workers, the foragers, leave the nest to collect resources, so trophallaxis ensures that all colony members receive food.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about trophallaxis function

claim: The experiment manipulated the nests of Camponotus pennsylvanicus by quadrupling the available nest space.

To do this, we filmed three colonies under high-density conditions for four hours each (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) before quadrupling the available nest space.
